title: US tightens rules on chip exports. But divisions over AI and China persist.
text:
US tightens rules on chip exports. But divisions over AI and China persist.
The new export-control rules released by the Commerce Department close a loophole that had allowed Nvidia and other companies to supply chips to offshore data centers used by Chinese companies that can’t legally buy advanced U.S. chips.
The recent scandal at Nvidia and revelations about China’s efforts to obtain advanced U.S. chips has shone a spotlight on the tension between national security and commercial incentives in the tech industry.
This week, the Trump administration announced new export-control rules for computing chips, following tumult at Nvidia, which designs chips used to train artificial intelligence models. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s founder and CEO, resigned last week after admitting to an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy at a Singapore-based company that is under investigation in the U.S. over its role in diverting advanced AI chips to China.
The new rules released by the Commerce Department will close a loophole that had allowed Nvidia and other companies to supply chips to offshore data centers, mostly in southeast Asia, which were then used by Chinese companies that can’t legally buy advanced U.S. chips.
The scandal at Nvidia has put a spotlight on the tension between national security and commercial incentives in the tech industry. Congress is now considering legislation to govern the export of advanced AI technology.
China hawks in Washington have long denounced these data centers in Singapore, Malaysia, and other countries as a backdoor for China to circumvent export controls and advance its AI capacity. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had reportedly slow-walked the new rules and sided with Mr. Huang, who claimed tighter restrictions would incentivize China to develop its own AI chips, and that China’s reliance on American AI hardware is in the United States’ strategic interest.
In recent days, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has publicly criticized Mr. Lutnick and Nvidia for resisting regulations and ignoring alleged smuggling of chips by Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company where the woman who had the alleged affair with Mr. Huang worked. The open feuding within the administration comes as Mr. Trump travels to Asia, where he is due to meet on Thursday with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Congress is now demanding answers from Mr. Huang and Trump administration officials, and is considering legislation to govern the export of advanced AI technology.
The administration’s new rules “are a good step in the right direction,” says Emily Kilcrease, a former deputy assistant U.S. trade representative under the first Trump administration who worked on export controls. But “I think the conversation is far from over.”
What are the new export rules?
Data centers that provide large-scale computing services to China-based companies must now obtain export licenses within 90 days or face restrictions on the procurement of U.S.-designed chips. Companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, and Brazil are subject to additional export-licensing restrictions because of a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” of advanced chips to China, according to the new rule.
Experts say these controls should be effective in closing a loophole by which Chinese AI companies could train their models remotely on advanced chips. The rules also will make it harder for Chinese entities to manufacture their own advanced AI semiconductors at cutting-edge facilities in Taiwan and South Korea that Nvidia uses for its production. Taiwan last year indicted an employee of TSMC, the largest chipmaker, for attempting to sell its manufacturing secrets to China. A Nvidia employee was also indicted in Taiwan for allegedly smuggling AI servers to China.
But some Democrats in Congress question whether they go far enough. The rules are “weaker than they should be,” says Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who has called on Mr. Lutnick to resign. He tells the Monitor that Mr. Lutnick “seemingly had a conflict of interest in scaling back the export controls and perhaps promoting the flow of high-power chips to China.” Mr. Lutnick’s former investment firm, which is now run by his sons, has interests in a range of industries connected to AI and chips.
What is the political dispute within the administration?
A conflict has erupted within the Trump administration over Nvidia’s dealings with Megaspeed, underscoring differing positions on the AI race with China. Megaspeed has been under investigation over export licensing violations since 2024 and was put on Nvidia’s own “no sell” list in June 2025. Mr. Bessent, along with Secretary of State Marco Rubio and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, had reportedly pushed to close the data centers loophole and blamed Mr. Lutnick for resisting tighter restrictions and failing to sanction Megaspeed. Other departments wanted to blacklist the Singaporean company, Mr. Bessent told CNBC last Friday. But the Commerce Department “has the pen” and ultimate authority over export rules.
The new rules on chip exports were released by the Commerce Department, but expressly say they were “written by and at the direction” of the Department of the Treasury and the National Security Council. This is unprecedented, noted Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. “That implies that Commerce was dragged kicking and screaming over the finish line by the White House and Treasury,” he wrote on X.
Asked by reporters about Mr. Bessent and Mr. Lutnick, both of whom are traveling with him to Asia, Mr. Trump on Monday framed the rift as a policy disagreement. “One wants to be friendly with China,” he said, referring to Mr. Lutnick, “and one wants to have a blowup with China.”
The president has built a personal relationship with Mr. Huang, whom he defended last week. He has repeatedly praised Nvidia, in which he owns millions of dollars in stock as part of a portfolio the White House says he doesn’t manage.
In May 2025, Mr. Trump reversed Biden-era restrictions on which chips Nvidia could export to China, a move Mr. Huang welcomed. Last December, the president announced plans to allow approved Chinese companies to buy a newer, more powerful chip, while keeping restrictions on Nvidia’s most cutting-edge technology. Nvidia is among the largest donors to Mr. Trump’s White House ballroom renovation project, contributing $25 million, The Washington Post reported last month. The company also donated to his inauguration fund.
What is Congress doing on this issue?
There is broad support on both sides of the aisle in Congress for investigations into Nvidia and for tightening regulations. “I think export controls, especially not selling high-end manufacturing equipment to communist China, has got broad bipartisan support,” GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts of Nebraska told reporters on Tuesday.
Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana struck an even more critical note. “It’s clear to me that the Department of Commerce has been allowing China to circumvent our export controls, and I want to know why, and I want to know how, and I want to know what we’re going to do to stop it,” he told reporters.
Democrats are expected to step up congressional investigations after they take control in January. Some are starting to look at Nvidia-related conflicts of interest in the Trump administration and Mr. Trump’s close ties with Mr. Huang.
Mr. Lutnick is due to appear before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10. His deputy, Jeffrey Kessler, who oversees export controls, has also been asked to testify. The Senate Banking Committee is one of several in the House and Senate that have requested briefings from Mr. Huang and Nvidia’s general counsel. (Nvidia announced Monday that it had set up a committee to oversee compliance with national security and export control regulations.)
Several bills related to export controls on AI equipment and semiconductors have already been introduced in Congress. Some Democrats want to attach them to a must-pass defense appropriations bill as a way to pressure the White House.
It’s important that Congress authorize “the strongest litigation-proof authority as possible” for regulators, says Ms. Kilcrease, who directs the energy, economics, and security program at the Center for a New American Security, a think tank in Washington. She adds, “I’m not sure how much I trust the administration on export controls right now.”
Simon Montlake reported from Boston and Victoria Hoffmann reported from Washington.
